How the interview runs (sourced)

The PayPal SQL interview, as candidates report it

PayPal does not publish the format. Each row is what candidates and prep guides have described publicly, with its source; where sources disagree, the row says so. Formats change — treat every specific as reported, not official.

Roles where SQL is testedData Science, Data Engineering and Data Analytics.[1]
Data scientist processA prep guide describes four to five rounds over three to four weeks, including a live SQL and Python round of 45–60 minutes on a shared screen. The guide does not say where its round descriptions come from.[6]
Phone roundsOne data scientist report (interview December 2025) describes a 15-minute recruiter call, then two one-hour phone rounds: SQL and Python with a short case, then statistics and causal inference. Its one SQL question carried many filter conditions, and where each sat — WHERE or the join's ON — mattered.[5]
OnsiteAnother data scientist report (interview July 2025) describes three back-to-back onsite rounds: two on fraud and risk decisions, one of three SQL questions in which the interviewer asked for conditional aggregation with CASE WHEN rather than a plain sum.[4]
Data analyst internA 2023 report describes a one-hour HackerRank assessment (ten multiple-choice questions across ML, SQL, probability and statistics, plus one Python question), then a technical round with one SQL query in a HackerRank editor, and a hiring-manager round with SQL the candidate called medium to tough.[3]
What is not settledThe reports span 2023 to 2025, intern to experienced, and different teams; no source states one format for every PayPal data role. Only the intern report says the code was run (against test cases). (no reliable source)

One data scientist report describes onsite rounds on fraud and risk decisions, one of them a fraud-labelling case; another puts a short case inside a phone round.[4][5] Their loop reportedly includes a metrics/case round — practise it here (the first 3 questions are free, the rest is Pro).

The SQL that comes up

What PayPal SQL questions test

Reported most often, in order

  • 1Conditional aggregation (CASE WHEN inside SUM or COUNT)
  • 2Aggregates in HAVING
  • 3Joins, and filters in WHERE vs ON
  • 4Ranking with ties (average transaction per user)
  • 5Funnels and conversion rates
  • 6Transaction-flow and segmentation analysis
  • 7Anomaly and data-quality checks on transactions

Difficulty: Reported as medium in a July 2025 onsite and hard, by the candidate's own account, in a December 2025 phone round; the 2023 intern report calls the hiring-manager SQL medium to tough. The data is payments between users (payer, recipient, amount), account transactions (deposits and withdrawals), and card transactions with merchants and risk flags.

Sample questions

PayPal SQL question shapes, and where to practise them

Shapes candidates and guides report (paraphrased)

  • Deposits and withdrawals per account: each account's closing balance.[2]
  • Payments from one user to another: how many pairs of users have sent money in both directions.[1]
  • Users with sign-up dates and their transactions: total and average spend per user, only for users with at least two transactions.[1]

Topic practice

Every challenge in the PayPal set, by topic

These are SQL Quest challenges matched to the topics candidates report for PayPal — not questions PayPal has asked.

Every query here runs on SQLite in your browser. Joins, GROUP BY, CTEs and window functions are written the same way in PostgreSQL, MySQL and Snowflake; dates are where they differ (SQLite's strftime('%Y-%m', ts) is to_char(ts, 'YYYY-MM') in PostgreSQL), and the app lists each difference beside every challenge.

Drill the skills the PayPal set leans on, one at a time: JOIN practice · GROUP BY exercises · CTE practice · CASE WHEN practice · Window function practice — or browse every SQL practice question.

Every question in the PayPal set, one page each with the schema and a hint: LEFT JOIN: Watch the NULLs Appear · Transaction Share by Merchant Category · Card Spend by Country · Transactions at High-Risk Merchants · Chargeback Reason Codes: Resolved and Still Open · Active Spender Cohort (HAVING) · Chargeback Rate Per Merchant · Ticket-Size Mix by Category · Cardholders Who Have Never Disputed a Charge · Spend and Disputes Per Cardholder — Without the Fan-Out · Busiest Merchants, and What a Tie Does to the Rank · Order Funnel Conversion · 3-Sigma Anomaly: Transaction Amount Outliers · Velocity Rule — 5+ Transactions in 5 Minutes · Two Swipes at the Same Merchant Inside a Day · Disputed Spend by Risk Tier and Category.
